name: bluewater-11-he-called-back
lines: You sent the quote on Monday. Friday, she hired somebody else.
And you told yourself what everybody tells themselves. He must've been cheaper.
He wasn't.
The guy who got your job did one thing after the quote that you didn't.
He called back.
Let me walk you through it with Marcus. Marcus isn't a real person. I built him out of a hundred real ones.
He builds decks. Eleven years. Best work on the street, and the neighbours know it.
Monday, he measures a backyard. The homeowner wants it done before summer.
That night he sends the quote. Say fourteen thousand dollars. Fair. Detailed. Photos of his last three decks.
Then he does what almost every good tradesman does next.
Nothing.
She's got my number, he thinks. If she wants it, she'll call.
And if you asked him why he didn't call her, he'd tell you the truth. He doesn't want to be that guy. The pushy one.
He's a builder. His work should speak for itself.
It would. If she ever saw it.
Tuesday, nothing. Wednesday, nothing. By Friday he's writing the next quote, and he's forgotten this one.
Now look at her week.
Three quotes on the kitchen counter. Two kids. A job. And a husband who wants to think about it.
She isn't ignoring Marcus. She's busy. His quote is under a pizza menu.
Wednesday afternoon, her phone buzzes. It's one of the other builders.
Hi, it's Walt. Any questions on the deck quote? Happy to walk you through it.
She does have a question. He answers it in four minutes.
Friday, she signs with Walt. And Walt's price was higher. By twelve hundred dollars.
Marcus never found out. He just never heard back. So he filed it under price.
Here's what that costs. Say Marcus writes eight quotes a month and wins two.
Six go quiet. Say a call back wins just one more of those six.
One more deck a month. A hundred and sixty eight thousand dollars a year. For a few text messages.
I made those numbers up. Put your own in. It won't come out to zero.
Here's the thing nobody told you.
Silence isn't a no. Silence is a person having a busy week.
And a quote with no follow up isn't a quote. It's a flyer.
So here are three moves. None of them is pushy. None of them costs a cent.
Move one. Set up the call back before you leave the driveway.
Say this. I'll send the quote tonight, and I'll check in Thursday. Does that work?
She says sure. Now Thursday's call isn't chasing. It's keeping your word.
Put it in your phone before you start the truck.
Move two. Day two, send one short message. And never ask, did you get my quote?
Give her one useful thing instead. Something like, the price includes hauling the old deck away. Any questions?
It's two lines. And it puts your quote back on top of the pile.
Move three. Day seven, give her the easy way out.
No pressure at all. Are you still thinking about the deck, or should I close your file?
People tend to answer that one. And either answer helps you. A yes is a job. A no is a clear desk.
Then keep one list. Every open quote, and the date of your next message. That's the whole system.
And if that still feels pushy, think about it this way. Pushy is ten calls. This is three messages in a week, and she agreed to the first one.
Now, the trap. Don't chase with a discount.
The second you knock off five hundred dollars nobody asked for, you've told her the first price wasn't real.
And don't follow up forever. Three touches. Then wish her well and move on.
So, a month later. Another backyard. Another Monday.
Marcus measures. And on his way out he says, I'll check in Thursday.
Thursday, he does.
Oh good, she says. I had a question about the railing.
Friday, signed. The same price he would've quoted anyway.
And that night, his phone buzzes again.
It's a quote from six weeks ago. The one he sent the day seven message to.
Are you still building decks? We're finally ready.
I can't promise a call back wins you the job. Nobody can.
Some people were never going to hire you. You'll just find out faster.
But you'll stop losing the ones who were.
So do this tonight.
Scroll back thirty days. Find every quote that went quiet.
Send each one two lines. No discount. Just, still thinking about it, or should I close your file?
Then watch your phone on Friday.
Marcus's number was a hundred and sixty eight thousand. Yours is sitting in your sent folder.
And if you'd rather your follow up ran without you, that's something we set up. The link's in the description.
